profile.story: Loomcraft sells hand-loomed rugs, throws and table linens direct to consumers, made by two weaving cooperatives in Rajasthan and warehoused with a 3PL in Memphis. Revenue looks healthy at $3.4M and the brand has real repeat customers, but the money is all sitting in containers: Priya writes a purchase order six months before she can sell the goods, and a line of credit plus a supplier term extension is carrying the gap. The operations side is entirely manual — Shopify, the 3PL portal and QuickBooks do not talk, so two people spend most of their week retyping orders, chasing exceptions and reconciling inventory that never quite matches. A big spring buy is due in November and she does not know where the cash comes from.

intake.q2: We design and sell hand-loomed rugs, throws, cushion covers and table linens directly to consumers through our own site, with a small wholesale line into about 40 independent home stores. Everything is made by two weaving cooperatives we have worked with since 2017 and shipped from a third-party warehouse in Memphis. Eleven of us: three in marketing, two in customer experience, two in operations, a designer, a wholesale rep, a part-time bookkeeper and me.
intake.q5: Same revenue would be fine if it converted to cash. I want the spring buy funded from operations rather than the credit line, order flow that runs itself, and a wholesale channel big enough to smooth the seasonality. My role should be product and brand, not order exceptions.

P1.note: Five sources with monthly volume, cost and quality in the Shopify/GA4 exports (q23: paid social 1,650 at $26K, organic 1,180, email 690, affiliate 190, wholesale 90); reviewed weekly in the marketing meeting.
P1.why_not_higher: Wholesale is untracked by her own answer, and the tracking that exists is reviewed by channel spend, not by contribution — anchor 4 needs cost and quality reviewed together monthly across all sources.

P2.note: Orders land in Shopify automatically; anything unusual falls into an exception queue worked twice a day, watched live at 22 orders in 41 minutes. Customer email sits in a shared inbox connected to nothing (q24).
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs every inquiry captured in one system; the support inbox is outside every system and wholesale inquiries wait up to two days.

P3.note: Abandoned-cart flow gives three automated touches on retail and was shown firing in Klaviyo; wholesale inquiries get one touch 'if Ruth is not travelling' (q24).
P3.why_not_higher: The sequence covers only the retail half — anchor 3 needs a defined sequence used on most leads, and the higher-value half of the funnel has none.

P4.note: Checkout completion 33% is tracked, but q25 says wholesale has no process at all and Ruth improvises; there are no stages and no loss-reason capture outside the site analytics.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a loose process across the business; on the wholesale side there is nothing at all, and retail conversion is a site metric rather than a sales process.

P5.note: Price lists on file dated 2024. Q28 says pricing is based on job economics and competitor sets, but the economics are a quarterly SKU spreadsheet with freight allocated by guess (q17) — the $84K air freight run went straight to profit, not to price.
P5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs real economics behind the price with occasional reviews; the input costs have moved and the prices have not since 2024.

P6.note: Rug pads and cleaning kits offered at checkout, a room bundle exists, a limited collection twice a year and an entry price point (q29).
P6.why_not_higher: Her own answer says the bundle was 'never merchandised properly' — anchor 3 needs the tiers and upsell actually presented on the core offer, and the highest-attachment product is only shown at the last step.

P7.note: Cohort export measures a 27% second-purchase rate and identifies 5,800 one-time buyers dormant 24+ months. One win-back email in 2025, never repeated (q27).
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the inactive list worked at least twice a year; it has been worked once in two years and then abandoned on margin grounds.

P8.note: Tomas owns marketing, Ruth owns wholesale, and CAC and conversion are reviewed weekly (q30).
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs leads, conversion and value reviewed monthly by named owners — wholesale is never in the same conversation and 'nobody agrees on the definition' of lifetime value.

P9.note: P&L gives 44% company gross margin, but q17 confirms the by-SKU view is a quarterly spreadsheet with freight allocated by guess — so the margin on the 48% of revenue that is rugs is not actually known.
P9.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the overall margin known and reliable; here the freight and duty that move it most are not allocated at all, which is how an $84K air freight run became a surprise.

P10.note: Q20 monthly-delayed; the monthly close waits on an inventory valuation that takes days to reconcile, and cash is managed off a spreadsheet Priya maintains by hand (walked in session).
P10.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs monthly-ish financials that are lightly used; here the number that matters most — cash — is not in the financials at all, it is in a personal spreadsheet.

S1.note: Q50 keeps purchasing, pricing, escalations, hiring, banking, vendors, technical decisions and strategy with Priya; only Tomas has authority, capped at $5K of ad spend (q51).
S1.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs several areas genuinely delegated; one capped spending authority in one function is not several.

S2.note: Four-week test (q51): the site and ads run, exceptions degrade within two days, and purchase orders, the credit line and inventory reconciliation stop entirely.
S2.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the business to run short-term while decisions stack up; here the supply chain stops in week one, which is bleeding rather than slowing.

S3.note: The site sells without her and Ruth owns the wholesale accounts end to end; only 7% of revenue rides on Priya's own relationships (q14).
S3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs standard deals closed by the team with the owner on the largest few; the supplier side — which is where the real relationship risk sits — is entirely hers.

S4.note: Two leads on paper (q10) but q38 says roles are informal and q34 rates defined handoffs and exception escalation as 'rarely' consistent.
S4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some real managers with patchy accountability; here only marketing has an owner who owns a number, and nobody watches an operational one (q39).

S5.note: Drive folder opened in session: four procedure documents, none covering exceptions or inventory — the two processes the business runs on. Q35 puts documented at 30% and current at 15%.
S5.why_not_higher: Not current, not trained from, and the critical workflows are the undocumented ones.

S6.note: Q40 biweekly-to-monthly; the only regular meeting is marketing's, with three KPIs all owned by the same person and targets visible only in that room (q39).
S6.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs meetings to happen with a few KPIs and loose follow-through; operations — where the constraint is — has no meeting and no number.

S7.note: About 18% of orders hit an exception (q4) and q36 lists missed handoffs, rework and incomplete information as recurring. Q31 says a 20% jump needs capital, not effort.
S7.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs delivery to be mostly consistent with growth needing heroics; here the heroics are already running at current volume.

S8.note: Cohort and channel export: largest wholesale account 12% of revenue, top five 21%, with 93% of revenue spread across 21,400 retail buyers.
S8.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs the largest under 10%; at 12% this is a broad base with one account that would still be missed.

S9.note: No contracted or recurring revenue at all (q12: 69% products, 31% repeat without contract); the cohort export gives a 27% second-purchase rate, so repeat exists but nothing is committed.
S9.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some repeat or contract revenue in a form you can forecast from; a 27% repeat rate with no subscription and violent seasonality is closer to hope than to a base.

S10.note: Vendor agreements written, licences current, company owns its IP and accounts (q53). Q52 names the cooperatives, the credit line, Marisol and the single 3PL as known, unaddressed exposures.
S10.why_not_higher: No cross-training on the exception or inventory process, no second supplier or warehouse, and no continuity plan — anchor 3 needs cross-training started.

L1.note: Shopify, Klaviyo, the 3PL portal, QuickBooks and Gusto are real systems and were walked in session (q41).
L1.why_not_higher: Two big gaps rather than one: wholesale runs on a Google Sheet and email, and reporting runs on a spreadsheet Priya maintains — anchor 3 allows one.

L2.note: Q42 'one person is the integration', confirmed on the tour: Shopify → 3PL portal → QuickBooks with Marisol and Priya retyping at every join, and 38 SKUs out of agreement in the live reconciliation.
L2.why_not_higher: The 0 anchor verbatim — the same data is typed into several places and a person is the glue.

L3.note: Q43 claims accurate data, but the live reconciliation put Shopify and the 3PL 38 SKUs apart, and the number the business is actually run on — cash — lives in a hand-built spreadsheet outside every system.
L3.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the numbers mostly right after cleanup; inventory does not survive cleanup, and there is one report anyone fully trusts.

L4.note: 44 h/wk inventoried in q44 and confirmed in b4, 17 of it on Marisol alone. Nothing operational has been reduced — the load is acknowledged in q4's own target and untouched.
L4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a few fixes made; every fix made so far is in marketing, and none of it touched the operational load.

L5.note: Klaviyo welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase and review flows shown firing and genuinely reliable; ad reporting automated (q45).
L5.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs automations in several functions; every automation in this business is in one function, and nobody is named as its owner.

L6.note: Q46: drafting, marketing content and customer communication — the marketing team uses it daily for copy and Jae drafts support replies with it.
L6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs AI inside one or two defined workflows; here it is individual use across two teams with no workflow depending on it.

L7.note: Q47 returns one of eight — someone accountable per implementation. No data rules, no review rule, nothing measured, nothing documented before it was automated.
L7.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs several practices however inconsistent; one is not several, particularly with customer data already flowing through the shared inbox.

L8.note: Q48: shared passwords and unclear access on the 3PL and ad accounts, inconsistent backups, single-vendor dependence; q43 does confirm the team knows where sensitive data lives and backups exist.
L8.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs access controlled and off-boarding done; shared logins on the warehouse portal are exactly the known gap that keeps this at partial hygiene.

L9.note: Q58 'pockets of capability'; q59 names marketing as self-sufficient in Klaviyo, operations as willing but with no time, and the bookkeeper as resistant.
L9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the team trained on the core tools; the operations half — where the work is — has had no training on anything.

L10.note: Q49: $12–18K 'depends on how November goes', 3 owner hours, and team hours available only after the spring buy ships; q55 says cash must be resolved first.
L10.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs limited but real capacity; here both the budget and the hours are explicitly conditional on a cash event that has not happened.

assessment.owner_objective: More profit & cash flow — then Better operations & delivery capacity, Use AI/automation effectively
assessment.owner_belief: Cash. We are profitable on paper and I still cannot sleep in October. Everything I make goes back into containers six months before I can sell it, and this year the spring buy and the credit line renewal land in the same month. It has been getting worse every year since we added the wholesale line.
assessment.primary_constraint: Cash is trapped in inventory the business cannot see accurately: Shopify, the 3PL and QuickBooks are joined by two people retyping, so demand planning, purchasing and pricing are all decided off numbers that do not agree — and the buffer for that error is bought with the credit line.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: 38 SKUs out of agreement in a single live reconciliation; an $84K emergency air freight run to cover a stockout; about 18% of orders hitting a manual exception queue; a 148-day cash conversion cycle; freight allocated by guess so the rug line's real margin is unknown; the owner reconciling inventory herself seven hours a week.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$84K of one-off air freight and expedite cost in the last twelve months, on the P&L · ~$66K of operations and customer-experience payroll on 44 weekly hours of manual order work · ~364 owner hours a year on inventory reconciliation.
assessment.constraint_fix: A real inventory sync between Shopify and the 3PL with exception rules that resolve the common cases automatically, freight and duty landed into SKU cost so margin and price are decided on the true number, and a rolling 13-week cash view that includes the purchase-order calendar.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Land freight and duty into SKU cost and reprice the rug line against it — a decision inside her control, visible on the November buy, and the input to everything else on the list.

opportunities.title: Sync inventory and automate the order exception queue
opportunities.finding: Order exception triage and inventory reconciliation take 19 hours a week between Marisol and Priya (q44, confirmed live at 22 orders in 41 minutes and 38 SKUs out of agreement). The fix removes most of that work — but this is deliberately priced at zero dollars: the hours come back to an operations coordinator who is already behind and to the owner, not to payroll that gets removed or to revenue work. The report should print recovered capacity, not cash. If those hours are later redeployed onto wholesale account management, this gets re-priced then.
opportunities.blueprint: Real-time inventory sync between Shopify and the 3PL, automated rules for the four exception types that make up most of the queue (backorder, split shipment, address failure, wholesale terms), and a daily variance report instead of a manual count.
opportunities.replaces: Two people retyping between three systems twice a day

opportunities.title: Reprice on landed cost, starting with the rug line
opportunities.finding: Gross margin is 44% on the P&L against a 46% target that has never been hit, and q17 confirms freight and duty are allocated by guess — so the rug line, 48% of revenue, is priced without knowing what it costs. The $84K air freight run sits on the P&L as a one-off; it is really a pricing input. A modest move on rugs and throws with landed cost underneath it.
opportunities.blueprint: Landed-cost model per SKU including ocean freight, duty and 3PL handling; reprice rugs and throws against it; move the shipping threshold so the checkout loss reason she named stops being subsidised out of margin.
opportunities.replaces: A 2024 price list and freight allocated by guess

opportunities.title: Bring back the 5,800 customers who bought once and never returned
opportunities.finding: The Shopify cohort export identifies 5,800 buyers with one order and nothing in 24 months, against a 27% second-purchase rate on the customers who do come back. One win-back email ran in 2025 and was dropped because the discount hurt margin — which is a reason to change the offer, not to stop. Q27 names the real problem: 'there is no reason for them to come back unless we give them one.'
opportunities.blueprint: Segment the dormant cohort by first-purchase category, run a three-touch Klaviyo sequence built on the new collection and the room bundle rather than on discount, and merchandise cushion covers and linens as the second purchase for rug buyers.
opportunities.replaces: A single discounted win-back email in 2025

expected_warnings: one opportunity above 50% of the raw expected total — the dormant-cohort reactivation carries about 52% of the projected recovery, because the third finding is deliberately priced at $0 as capacity
